transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-24 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Ortiz (Redwood AE), Ravi Kumar (Redwood SE), Elena Park (CTO, Cinder Labs), Marcus Lee (Head Infra), Samira Osei (ML Eng)
---
Summary: intake call focused on dedicated capacity. Main themes: tenant sharding for isolation, burst SLA (short spikes to 3x baseline), fallback model variants and regional failover, security/compliance (SOC2, KMS), and a benchmark/pilot to validate latency & cost.
Topics: dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, prewarm/warm pools, KV cache behavior across tenant shards, network topology (VPC peering vs private link), and contract/SLA expectations.
Action items: see metadata list above.
---
Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Ortiz: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um I'm Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account. quick intros, Ravi is our solutions engineer, he'll jump into the capacity sizing stuff. Elena, want to kick off with a bit about what you're trying to solve?
[00:18] Elena Park: yeah thanks Maya. so Cinder builds an AI assistant that summarizes and annotates legal docs for enterprise clients. latency is like, pretty important for live sessions and some batch jobs. we're evaluating whether to go Redwood hosted to move fast versus dedicated capacity because of tenant isolation and predictable cost.
[00:36] Marcus Lee: and for infra side we care about tenant isolation — we have customers that require strict data isolation and resident logs. also need to understand prewarm times and how bursts are handled, we sometimes see short spikes during onboarding that are 2–3x baseline for 10–45 minutes.
[00:52] Ravi Kumar: cool, thanks. quick clarification — when you say tenant isolation, do you mean logical multi-tenant separation on shared infra, or completely dedicated nodes per customer?
[01:05] Elena Park: good question. baseline: we want logical isolation per our SLAs, but for a handful of our top customers we may need physical isolation (dedicated nodes) or at least cgroup/tenant fencing. privacy regs push us there.
[01:18] Samira Osei: yeah and also from model behavior, we rely on KV cache to preserve context between user interactions; we need to know if that cache is per-tenant and how it survives scale-out/back.
[01:30] Maya Ortiz: perfect. that's exactly the sort of thing Redwood Dedicated is designed for — you can reserve GPU pools with tenancy policies and govern prewarm pools. i'll hand it over to Ravi to run through the technical model for burst and fallback.
[01:40] Ravi Kumar: thanks. quick overview: dedicated pools can be carved into tenant shards — think of logical shards that pin work to a subset of GPUs to reduce cross-tenant noisy neighbor risk. we also support physical isolation where you reserve whole nodes for a tenant. for bursts we offer a warm pool and a burst reserve; warm pool keeps a subset prewarmed (reduced KV rebuild) and burst reserve can spin up extra nodes but with a slightly longer lead time.
[02:05] Marcus Lee: what's the lead time for a burst node? are we talking seconds or minutes?
[02:12] Ravi Kumar: warm pool responds in seconds — typically 5–20s for small scale increments. burst reserve (cold) is minutes — usually 3–8 minutes depending on region and GPU type. those numbers vary with sequence length and model size.
[02:28] Elena Park: 3–8 minutes could be concerning for live sessions. we need an SLA for those customer-facing spikes. can you offer a burst SLA guaranteeing prewarm within X minutes?
[02:40] Maya Ortiz: we have tiered burst SLAs on our enterprise contracts — a hard SLA is doable for dedicated customers if you reserve burst capacity as part of the commitment. we'll surface a sample SLA in the docs — typically it ties to a guaranteed warm pool size and a max provisioning time for burst nodes.
[02:56] Samira Osei: and if the burst fails, what's the fallback? like do we get degraded latency with a smaller model, or do you queue requests?
[03:06] Ravi Kumar: great question. we have configurable fallback policies — automatic downgrade to a quantized variant of the model (slower quality but faster startup), or regional failover to another pool if cross-region is allowed. we also support graceful shedding where low-priority requests are delayed or rejected based on route.
[03:24] Marcus Lee: is the quantized variant something we control? we need to ensure output quality doesn't break contracts.
[03:31] Ravi Kumar: you can pin a model family and specify allowable variants for fallback. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles based on your prompts so you can understand quality delta. we'll run a small eval as part of the pilot.
[03:46] Elena Park: ok we like that. can you explain the KV cache story when you shard tenants? does cache live on the same GPU and is it lost if we route to a different shard?
[03:56] Ravi Kumar: KV cache is local to the worker instance. if we route to a different shard that doesn't have the KV, we reconstruct from stored context (prefix caching or persistent short-term KV). we also support sticky routing so sessions remain pinned to a shard for X minutes; that's configurable. the tradeoff is resource utilization versus cache hit rate.
[04:22] Samira Osei: sticky routing seems crucial for our UX. what's the default sticky timeout?
[04:27] Ravi Kumar: default is 10 minutes, can be extended. longer stickiness reduces cross-shard overhead but can lead to imbalanced utilization. we'll include utilization modelling in the capacity calc.
[04:40] Marcus Lee: network question — we have strict network policies. do you support VPC peering or private link, and how does egress behave?
[04:49] Maya Ortiz: both. Dedicated can run in your VPC (Redwood Private control plane) or we can peer to your VPC in the cloud; HSM/KMS integrations for key wrapping are available. we'll send you a network diagram and sample IP ranges.
[05:02] Elena Park: SOC2/ISO? audit logs? we have customers requiring these for legal review.
[05:07] Maya Ortiz: we are SOC2 Type II and have ISO documentation. we provide audit logs, per-route token billing, and can forward logs to your SIEM for retention. full details in the security pack i'll share.
[05:18] Marcus Lee: good. and billing — if we reserve burst capacity but don't use it, what's the model?
[05:25] Maya Ortiz: reserved capacity has a baseline monthly charge; burst reserve is part of the commitment but priced lower than always-on. unused reserved burst capacity is billed at a reduced rate per the contract; we also have rollover options depending on term length. we'll include sample math in the pricing sheet.
[05:39] Samira Osei: about the pilot — we want to run internal benchmarks with our production traces. can Redwood host a 48-hour benchmark with dedicated nodes?
[05:48] Ravi Kumar: yes — we can provision a dedicated pilot cluster for 48–72 hours and run through your traces. we'll instrument token-level latency, p95/p99, GPU utilization, and KV cache hit rates. we'll need the traces and expected concurrency profile.
[06:03] Elena Park: perfect, we'll extract traces. also curious about canary deploys — when you roll model updates, what's the safe path? we can't have regressions for customers in production.
[06:12] Ravi Kumar: our rollout supports canary percentages by route and automatic rollback on quality or latency regressions. we can tie regressions to eval suites you define; Redwood Optimize can run diffs on your prompt set.
[06:26] Marcus Lee: you mentioned region failover — do you replicate KV across regions or is that eventual? cross-region KV replication seems expensive.
[06:36] Ravi Kumar: we don't replicate full KV across regions by default. common approach: session affinity within region and checkpointing important context to a regionally replicated store. for strict multi-region high availability we can design a hybrid strategy, but yes it adds cost.
[06:50] Elena Park: another compliance point — can you support customer-managed keys in a customer KMS/HSM?
[06:56] Maya Ortiz: yes, we support customer-managed keys via KMS integrations and HSM for private deployments. key material never leaves your control for those flows. we'll include integration guide.
[07:07] Samira Osei: what about observability? we need per-tenant dashboards and tracing down to token latency for SLA breaches.
[07:15] Ravi Kumar: Redwood Console provides per-route & per-model dashboards, token-level histograms, and we're able to export traces to Jaeger/Zipkin or your SIEM. Token-level forensics are available — sample screenshots in the security deck.
[07:28] Elena Park: perfect. would you be able to share a sample SLA that guarantees p99 under X ms for certain reserved capacity?
[07:35] Maya Ortiz: yes, we'll send a sample SLA tailored to expected baseline/reserved and burst profile. typically p99 guarantees are tied to reserved warm pool sizes and defined fallback behaviors.
[07:48] Marcus Lee: what about cold start times for large models (40B+). we use a mix of 7B and 33B in prod.
[07:56] Ravi Kumar: for larger models cold start is longer — 33B, depending on quantization, is in the 30s-to-2m cold start range if you have to reload weights on a node. warm pools for frequently used models are recommended. we can also keep shard-local model mirrors pinned to reduce reload times.
[08:14] Samira Osei: and memory pressure — if multiple tenants burst at same time, do you allow preemption or capacity sharing?
[08:22] Ravi Kumar: there are policies: preemption (higher-tier tenants preempt lower), fair-share with soft limits, or strict isolation. choice is contractual. many customers pick hybrid: strict isolation for top customers and fair-share for the rest.
[08:38] Elena Park: sounds good. one more: what's the typical MTTR for node failures in dedicated pools?
[08:43] Ravi Kumar: automatic failover is within minutes and we replace nodes per SLA; the platform has health checks and a rebuild pipeline — MTTR for replacement is usually 5–20 minutes depending on region.
[08:56] Marcus Lee: ok. switching gears — we have some customers in EU and we need data residency. any issue with region-specific deployments?
[09:03] Maya Ortiz: we have regional deployments in EU/NA and can set data residency. private deployments allow on-prem if needed for stricter regs.
[09:11] Samira Osei: cost modelling — can you show token-level unit cost under a reserved plan vs hosted?
[09:18] Maya Ortiz: yes, that's part of the pricing sheet. reserved plans reduce unit cost, we can model at your throughput and token distribution. Ravi will run sims.
[09:27] Ravi Kumar: i'll run a sim using your trace once you share it. i'll include p95/p99 latency sensitivity to warm pool size.
[09:34] Elena Park: competition: we've also talked to InferScale and CloudModelHub; main differentiators for us are predictable latency, auditability, and predictable unit cost.
[09:44] Maya Ortiz: noted. Redwood's focus on production economics and unified tooling across hosted/dedicated/private is something we emphasize in those comparisons.
[09:53] Marcus Lee: okay next steps recap?
[09:56] Maya Ortiz: recap — we will: send security materials (SOC2, ISO, KMS guide), send pricing & sample SLA, provision a pilot cluster for a benchmark window once traces are in, and Ravi will produce capacity/cost sims.
[10:10] Elena Park: that's great. can we aim to have the pricing and pilot schedule by Monday?
[10:15] Maya Ortiz: yes we'll aim for Monday (2027-06-28) for pricing and initial sims.
[10:21] Samira Osei: one last small question — when you do model rollbacks based on eval regressions, how fast is rollback? we need that timeframe for incident response.
[10:30] Ravi Kumar: rollbacks are automated and usually effective within 30–90 seconds for route-level rollbacks; cluster-level changes depend on model deploy time but can be kept minimal with pinned variants.
[10:42] Marcus Lee: nice. thanks all.
[10:45] Elena Park: thanks, appreciate it. we'll follow up with traces and a a checklist of compliance needs.
[10:52] Maya Ortiz: thanks everyone. we'll circulate notes and next steps.
